name: Bloom's Taxonomy
one_line_summary: Hierarchy of cognitive learning objectives from remembering through evaluating and creating.
extended_summary: Bloom's Taxonomy was developed by a committee of educators chaired by Benjamin Bloom at the University of Chicago, presented in the 1956 Taxonomy of Educational Objectives: The Classification of Educational Goals, Handbook I: Cognitive Domain. The committee — also including Max Englehart, Edward Furst, Walter Hill, and David Krathwohl — emerged from work at the American Psychological Association's 1948 convention seeking a common vocabulary for examination and curriculum specialists. The original taxonomy articulates six hierarchical levels of cognitive complexity: Knowledge (recall of facts), Comprehension (understanding meaning), Application (using knowledge in new situations), Analysis (breaking down information into parts and identifying relationships), Synthesis (combining elements to create something new), and Evaluation (judging value and quality). Each level subsumes the lower levels. Bloom's two further volumes addressed the Affective Domain (Krathwohl, Bloom, Masia, 1964 — receiving, responding, valuing, organizing, characterizing) and the Psychomotor Domain (handled by other authors including Simpson 1972 and Harrow 1972). The cognitive taxonomy became the most widely-used framework in instructional design and curriculum development globally, with its action-verb hierarchy ('list,' 'describe,' 'apply,' 'analyze,' 'create') becoming the standard vocabulary for writing learning objectives. Anderson and Krathwohl's 2001 Revised Taxonomy substantially updated the framework.
originators: Benjamin S. Bloom (committee chair); Max Englehart, Edward Furst, Walter Hill, David Krathwohl (committee members)
year_or_decade: 1956 (Cognitive Domain handbook); 1964 (Affective Domain)
core_components: Six hierarchical cognitive levels: Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Analysis, Synthesis, Evaluation; Each level subsumes lower levels; Action-verb hierarchy for objective-writing; Three domains: Cognitive (1956), Affective (1964, Krathwohl), Psychomotor (subsequent authors); Foundation for instructional design and curriculum standards; Distinction between lower-order and higher-order thinking skills
primary_use_case: Curriculum and instructional design; learning objective specification; assessment design; teacher training and professional development; foundation for state and national curriculum standards globally; widely-used framework for distinguishing depths of learning; pedagogical reference across K-12, higher education, and corporate training.
common_criticisms: Strict hierarchical structure has been challenged — empirical research suggests cognitive processes don't always proceed in the prescribed order, and 'higher' levels often invoke 'lower' levels recursively rather than building on completed lower-level work; the cognitive/affective/psychomotor separation underweights interactions among domains; the taxonomy's apparent rigor obscures the substantial subjectivity in classifying objectives — the same activity can be coded at different levels depending on context; cross-cultural validity has been contested; commercial certification and curriculum-mapping industry has produced bureaucratic compliance with verb-list checklists rather than substantive engagement with cognitive depth; the original Synthesis-Evaluation ordering was substantially revised by Anderson-Krathwohl 2001 (placing Create at top), suggesting the hierarchy was less settled than its widespread adoption suggested.
primary_sources: Bloom, B.S. (ed.) (1956). Taxonomy of Educational Objectives: The Classification of Educational Goals, Handbook I: Cognitive Domain; Krathwohl, D.R., Bloom, B.S. & Masia, B.B. (1964). Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, Handbook II: Affective Domain
siblings: Revised Bloom's Taxonomy; SOLO Taxonomy; Webb's Depth of Knowledge

name: Revised Bloom's Taxonomy
one_line_summary: Updated Bloom adding the knowledge dimension and reordering create as the top.
extended_summary: The Revised Bloom's Taxonomy was published by Lorin Anderson, David Krathwohl (an original 1956 committee member), and colleagues in 2001 as A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives. The revision made three principal changes. First, the cognitive process dimension's top two levels were swapped — Synthesis (renamed Create) moved above Evaluation (renamed Evaluate), reflecting the argument that creative production is cognitively more complex than evaluation against criteria. Second, the categories were renamed from nouns to verbs (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create), better aligning with how learning objectives are typically written. Third, and most substantively, a separate Knowledge dimension was added, distinguishing four types of knowledge (Factual, Conceptual, Procedural, Metacognitive), creating a two-dimensional taxonomy table. This produces a 6 × 4 = 24-cell matrix that allows objectives to be classified by both cognitive process and knowledge type — a more nuanced classification than the original one-dimensional hierarchy. The Revised Taxonomy is now the standard reference in most contemporary instructional-design contexts, though both versions remain in use, with the 1956 original retaining substantial usage particularly in legacy curriculum frameworks.
originators: Lorin W. Anderson; David R. Krathwohl (original 1956 committee member); committee of educators including Peter Airasian, Kathleen Cruikshank, Richard Mayer, Paul Pintrich, James Raths, Merlin Wittrock
year_or_decade: 2001 (publication of revised taxonomy)
core_components: Two-dimensional structure: Cognitive Process Dimension and Knowledge Dimension; Cognitive Process Dimension (verbs): Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create; Knowledge Dimension: Factual, Conceptual, Procedural, Metacognitive; 24-cell taxonomy table; Reordering: Create above Evaluate (vs original Synthesis below Evaluation); Verb-form labels (vs original noun-form); Application to objective specification, assessment, and curriculum alignment
primary_use_case: Standard contemporary reference for instructional design and curriculum development; learning objective writing using the cognitive-process-by-knowledge-type matrix; assessment design ensuring coverage across both dimensions; teacher training and professional development; foundation for many contemporary curriculum frameworks and standards.
common_criticisms: The reordering of Create above Evaluate is empirically contested — some cognitive scientists argue evaluation often requires more sophisticated cognition than creation, particularly when creation is novelty without standards; the four knowledge types (Factual, Conceptual, Procedural, Metacognitive) have substantial overlap and operationalization varies; the 24-cell matrix's apparent precision obscures continuing subjectivity in classification; coexistence of original and revised versions creates which-version-when confusion in literature and practice; commercial alignment and curriculum-mapping industry has produced bureaucratic compliance with the matrix without substantive engagement; like the original, hierarchical structure remains contested as cognitive processes don't always proceed in prescribed order.
primary_sources: Anderson, L.W. & Krathwohl, D.R. (eds.) (2001). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives
siblings: Bloom's Taxonomy; SOLO Taxonomy; Webb's Depth of Knowledge

name: SOLO Taxonomy
one_line_summary: Biggs' Structure of the Observed Learning Outcome from prestructural to extended abstract.
extended_summary: The SOLO Taxonomy (Structure of the Observed Learning Outcome) was developed by John Biggs and Kevin Collis at the University of Newcastle (Australia) and presented in their 1982 Evaluating the Quality of Learning: The SOLO Taxonomy. Unlike Bloom's Taxonomy, which classifies cognitive processes by type, SOLO classifies the structural complexity of learning outcomes themselves through five levels: Prestructural (the student misses the point or shows minimal understanding); Unistructural (focuses on a single relevant aspect); Multistructural (focuses on several relevant aspects but treats them as separate); Relational (integrates aspects into a coherent whole); and Extended Abstract (generalizes the structure to new domains, abstracts to higher-level principles, makes connections beyond the original frame). The model's distinctive contribution is treating learning quality as a question of structural complexity in the student's understanding — visible in how the student organizes and relates information — rather than as cognitive-process type. SOLO has been particularly influential in higher-education assessment and outcomes-based curriculum design, including substantial use in Australia, New Zealand, and the UK. Pam Hook's subsequent application to K-12 classroom practice through HookED has substantially extended SOLO's reach. The framework pairs naturally with constructive alignment (Biggs's broader curriculum-design framework, in which intended outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment are deliberately aligned).
originators: John Biggs; Kevin Collis
year_or_decade: 1982 (foundational publication); 2003 (Biggs's Teaching for Quality Learning at University with SOLO and constructive alignment)
core_components: Five levels of structural complexity: Prestructural, Unistructural, Multistructural, Relational, Extended Abstract; Quantitative phase (uni-/multi-structural) and Qualitative phase (relational/extended abstract); Focus on outcome structure rather than process type; Distinction from Bloom's process-typology approach; Connection to Biggs's constructive alignment; Application in higher-education outcomes assessment; Pam Hook's K-12 extension through HookED
primary_use_case: Higher-education curriculum design and outcomes assessment; alternative or complement to Bloom's Taxonomy in objective specification; student self-assessment of understanding depth; teacher professional development; basis for outcomes-based education in Australia, New Zealand, UK; integration with constructive alignment for course design.
common_criticisms: Less widely adopted than Bloom's Taxonomy globally — particularly absent from US education contexts; classification of student responses can be subjective, with different graders coding the same response at different levels; the five-level structure may be too coarse for some assessment purposes and too fine for others; Extended Abstract level is rarely demonstrated in practice and may be aspirational; commercial branded extensions (HookED) vary in quality; like all hierarchical taxonomies, can become bureaucratic compliance with checklist application rather than substantive understanding of student work; works better in some disciplines (essay-based) than others (mathematical proof, code, performance arts).
primary_sources: Biggs, J.B. & Collis, K.F. (1982). Evaluating the Quality of Learning: The SOLO Taxonomy; Biggs, J.B. & Tang, C. (2011). Teaching for Quality Learning at University (4th ed.)
siblings: Bloom's Taxonomy; Revised Bloom's Taxonomy; Webb's Depth of Knowledge

name: Webb's Depth of Knowledge
one_line_summary: Four levels of cognitive complexity: recall, skill/concept, strategic thinking, extended thinking.
extended_summary: Webb's Depth of Knowledge (DoK) was developed by Norman Webb at the Wisconsin Center for Education Research, articulated in his 1997 monograph Criteria for Alignment of Expectations and Assessments in Mathematics and Science Education and elaborated in subsequent work. Webb developed DoK as an alignment tool — a way to evaluate whether assessment items and curriculum standards demanded the same cognitive complexity — distinguishing four levels: DoK 1 (Recall and Reproduction — facts, definitions, simple procedures); DoK 2 (Skills and Concepts — applying procedures, summarizing, classifying with multiple steps); DoK 3 (Strategic Thinking — non-routine reasoning, justification, multiple solution paths, supporting claims with evidence); DoK 4 (Extended Thinking — investigations or research extending across multiple sessions, connecting and applying ideas across content areas). The framework gained substantial adoption in US K-12 education through state and federal alignment requirements (No Child Left Behind, subsequent ESSA), with state assessment programs and curriculum frameworks frequently citing DoK levels as required complexity ranges. DoK is often paired or compared with Bloom's Taxonomy — they classify different things (DoK measures cognitive demand of the task; Bloom classifies cognitive process type), but in practice educators often use them similarly with substantial overlap.
originators: Norman L. Webb (Wisconsin Center for Education Research)
year_or_decade: 1997 (foundational monograph); ongoing refinement through 2000s
core_components: Four DoK levels: DoK 1 (Recall and Reproduction); DoK 2 (Skills and Concepts); DoK 3 (Strategic Thinking); DoK 4 (Extended Thinking); Focus on cognitive demand of task rather than student response (vs SOLO); Alignment-tool origin (matching assessment to standards); Distinction from Bloom's process typology; Adoption in US K-12 alignment frameworks; Often paired with Bloom in practice
primary_use_case: K-12 curriculum and assessment alignment in US education contexts; state assessment design and review; teacher professional development on cognitive demand of tasks; lesson and assessment design; foundation for many state standards-alignment documents; complement to Bloom's Taxonomy in instructional design.
common_criticisms: Often confused with Bloom's Taxonomy despite measuring different things — DoK measures task demand while Bloom classifies cognitive process type; classification of items into DoK levels is subjective, with different reviewers coding the same item differently; DoK 3 vs DoK 4 boundary is particularly contested; primarily a US K-12 framework with limited international adoption; commercial alignment-software industry produces bureaucratic compliance with DoK distributions ('your assessment must include 20% DoK 3 items') without substantive engagement; like Bloom, can become checklist application rather than substantive cognitive-demand analysis; DoK 4 (Extended Thinking) is rarely achievable in standardized assessment contexts which constrain its practical use.
primary_sources: Webb, N.L. (1997). Criteria for Alignment of Expectations and Assessments in Mathematics and Science Education; Webb, N.L. (2002). 'Depth of Knowledge Levels for Four Content Areas'
siblings: Bloom's Taxonomy; Revised Bloom's Taxonomy; SOLO Taxonomy

name: ADDIE Model
one_line_summary: Instructional design: Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate.
extended_summary: The ADDIE Model is the most widely-used instructional-design framework, structuring training and curriculum development through five sequential phases: Analyze (learner needs, audience, context, gaps, constraints); Design (learning objectives, sequencing, assessment strategy, instructional strategies); Develop (creation of materials, content, media, prototypes); Implement (delivery to learners, instructor training, infrastructure); Evaluate (formative evaluation throughout and summative evaluation after delivery, often via Kirkpatrick's four levels). The model's origins are not from a single author — it emerged from Florida State University's Center for Educational Technology in 1975 in work for the US Army's interservice training development, with no specific 'ADDIE inventor' claim. The original five-phase military model was iterative and contained substructure within each phase; the simplified linear ADDIE familiar in current corporate training was substantially developed through the 1990s. ADDIE has been the dominant framework in corporate training, military training, and higher education instructional design for decades, with Rapid Instructional Design (RID), Successive Approximation Model (SAM), and Agile Learning Design as more recent alternatives that respond to ADDIE's perceived rigidity and Waterfall-style sequencing.
originators: Florida State University's Center for Educational Technology (1975 ISD model for US Army); broader instructional-systems-design tradition; subsequent simplification by various practitioners
year_or_decade: 1975 (original FSU/Army ISD); 1990s (simplified linear ADDIE); ongoing use
core_components: Five phases: Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate; Sequential default flow with iterative variants; Connection to Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation (Reaction, Learning, Behavior, Results); Subsumes specific tasks: needs analysis, learner analysis, learning objectives, instructional strategies, materials production, delivery, assessment; Substantial commercial training and consulting ecosystem; Distinction from agile-style alternatives (SAM, AGILE-LD)
primary_use_case: Corporate training and L&D programs; military training development; higher-education course design; foundation for instructional-design certification (ATD, CPLP, others); reference framework in instructional-design education; basis for many learning-management-system content-development workflows.
common_criticisms: Sequential 'Waterfall' default produces design before implementation feedback, leading to costly rework when delivery reveals design problems; rigid phase structure ill-suited to rapidly-changing content (technology training, fast-evolving domains); evaluation as final phase under-emphasizes formative evaluation throughout development; substantial documentation overhead; the 'ADDIE inventor' is genuinely unclear and many adoptions invoke the framework as if it were a specific designer's intentional system; Successive Approximation Model (Allen 2003) and Agile Learning Design respond to perceived rigidity with iterative, prototype-based alternatives; commercial certification industry has produced compliance-style ADDIE practice that obscures the underlying flexibility.
primary_sources: Branson, R.K. et al. (1975). Interservice Procedures for Instructional Systems Development (FSU/Army origin); Gagne, R.M., Wager, W.W., Golas, K.C. & Keller, J.M. (2005). Principles of Instructional Design (5th ed.)
siblings: Backward Design; Universal Design for Learning

name: Backward Design
one_line_summary: Wiggins and McTighe: start with desired outcomes, then plan assessment, then instruction.
extended_summary: Backward Design (also Understanding by Design, UbD) was developed by Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe and presented in Understanding by Design (1998, expanded 2nd edition 2005). The framework inverts the traditional curriculum-design sequence (start with content or activities, design assessment last) by structuring design in three sequential stages: Stage 1 (Identify Desired Results — what students should know, understand, and be able to do; what 'enduring understandings' should remain after details are forgotten; what 'essential questions' should organize inquiry); Stage 2 (Determine Acceptable Evidence — what assessment evidence will demonstrate that the desired understandings have been achieved, designed before instructional planning to align assessment with intended outcomes); Stage 3 (Plan Learning Experiences and Instruction — design the activities and sequence backward from the assessment evidence). The framework's central insight is that planning instruction first tends to produce coverage-driven rather than understanding-driven curriculum — teachers cover content because it's in the curriculum, with assessment retrofitted afterward. Backward Design aligns intentions, evidence, and instruction explicitly. The framework includes the Six Facets of Understanding (explanation, interpretation, application, perspective, empathy, self-knowledge) as a substantive account of what counts as understanding beyond mere knowing. Backward Design is the dominant contemporary curriculum-design framework in K-12 US education and substantially influential in higher education.
originators: Grant Wiggins; Jay McTighe
year_or_decade: 1998 (Understanding by Design 1st ed); 2005 (expanded 2nd edition)
core_components: Three stages: Stage 1 Identify Desired Results; Stage 2 Determine Acceptable Evidence; Stage 3 Plan Learning Experiences; Enduring Understandings; Essential Questions; Six Facets of Understanding (explanation, interpretation, application, perspective, empathy, self-knowledge); Distinction from coverage-driven and activity-driven design; UbD planning templates; Connection to assessment-as-learning
primary_use_case: K-12 curriculum and unit design in US contexts; lesson planning and unit development; teacher professional development; foundation for many state and district curriculum frameworks; alternative to ADDIE for educator-led course design; substantial influence in higher-education course-design practice.
common_criticisms: Implementation in many schools has been substantially shallow — the language is adopted but the actual sequence (assessment design before instruction design) is often violated under time pressure; identifying genuine 'enduring understandings' requires deep disciplinary expertise that not all teachers have; commercial UbD certification and consulting industry has produced compliance-style adoption; tension with externally-mandated curriculum standards that constrain Stage 1; assessment-driven design risks reducing curriculum to what is testable; the Six Facets of Understanding overlap and operationalize unevenly; works better for content with stable disciplinary structure (math, history) than for emergent or interdisciplinary content; the framework's emphasis on understanding can be at odds with skill-based or competency-based curriculum needs.
primary_sources: Wiggins, G. & McTighe, J. (1998, 2nd ed. 2005). Understanding by Design
siblings: ADDIE Model; Universal Design for Learning

name: Universal Design for Learning
one_line_summary: Multiple means of engagement, representation, and action/expression.
extended_summary: Universal Design for Learning was developed by David Rose, Anne Meyer, and colleagues at CAST (Center for Applied Special Technology) beginning in the 1990s, drawing on the broader Universal Design movement in architecture (Ron Mace) and on neuroscience research on learner variability. UDL articulates three principles, each with specific guidelines: Multiple Means of Engagement (the why of learning — provide options for recruiting interest, sustaining effort, and self-regulation); Multiple Means of Representation (the what of learning — provide options for perception, language and symbols, and comprehension); Multiple Means of Action and Expression (the how of learning — provide options for physical action, expression and communication, and executive functions). The framework's central commitment is that learner variability is the norm rather than the exception, and that curriculum should be designed from the outset to accommodate variation rather than retrofitted with accommodations for individual learners. UDL has been substantially adopted in US K-12 education, particularly in special-education and inclusive-classroom contexts, and was specifically referenced in the 2008 Higher Education Opportunity Act. Empirical evidence on UDL outcomes is mixed — implementation quality varies substantially, and rigorous controlled research on UDL versus traditional design with appropriate accommodations is limited.
originators: David Rose; Anne Meyer; CAST (Center for Applied Special Technology); broader Universal Design movement (Ron Mace, North Carolina State)
year_or_decade: 1990s development; CAST UDL Guidelines published 2008 (1.0); 2018 (2.2 update); 2024 (3.0 update)
core_components: Three principles: Multiple Means of Engagement, Multiple Means of Representation, Multiple Means of Action and Expression; Specific guidelines under each principle; Foundation in learner-variability neuroscience; Connection to broader Universal Design (architecture, Ron Mace); Designed-in vs retrofitted accessibility; CAST UDL Guidelines as canonical reference; Application across K-12, higher education, and corporate learning
primary_use_case: Inclusive curriculum and instructional design, particularly in special-education and inclusive-classroom contexts; accessibility-first course development; teacher professional development on learner variability; foundation for some state and federal education policy on accessibility; growing application in higher education and online course design; integration with assistive technology design.
common_criticisms: Empirical evidence on UDL outcomes is mixed — implementation quality varies substantially, and rigorous controlled research on UDL versus traditional design with appropriate accommodations is limited; the framework's breadth (three principles, many guidelines) can produce checklist compliance without substantive learner-variability engagement; commercial UDL certification and consulting industry has shaped adoption; tension with content-coverage demands that limit time for multiple representations; misinterpretation as 'universal' when it is principally about anticipating typical variation, not literally accommodating every possible learner; some critics argue UDL underweights the difficulty of designing curriculum that genuinely works across substantial learner variability; recent 3.0 update reflects ongoing framework evolution that has sometimes felt like moving target for implementers.

siblings: Differentiated Instruction; ADDIE Model; Backward Design

name: Differentiated Instruction
one_line_summary: Tomlinson's approach tailoring content, process, product to learner readiness, interest, profile.
extended_summary: Differentiated Instruction was substantially developed and codified by Carol Ann Tomlinson at the University of Virginia, presented in The Differentiated Classroom (1999, 2nd ed. 2014) and How to Differentiate Instruction in Mixed-Ability Classrooms (1995, multiple editions). The framework articulates four classroom elements that can be differentiated — Content (what students learn), Process (how they engage with material), Product (how they demonstrate learning), and Learning Environment (the physical and social classroom climate) — in response to three student characteristics: Readiness (current skill level relative to objectives), Interest (engagement-driving topics), and Learning Profile (preferred ways of working, including but not limited to cultural and social factors). Differentiation is responsive — based on ongoing formative assessment of student readiness — rather than static. Differentiated Instruction is widely adopted in K-12 education, particularly in inclusive and mixed-ability classroom contexts, and shares common ground with UDL though with different design heritage (Tomlinson's framework emerged from gifted-education research; UDL from special-education and accessibility traditions). Empirical evidence on differentiated instruction's effectiveness is mixed and substantially dependent on implementation quality.
originators: Carol Ann Tomlinson
year_or_decade: 1995 (How to Differentiate Instruction); 1999 (The Differentiated Classroom); 2014 (2nd edition)
core_components: Four classroom elements differentiable: Content, Process, Product, Learning Environment; Three student characteristics: Readiness, Interest, Learning Profile; Responsive to ongoing formative assessment; Tiered assignments; Flexible grouping; Anchor activities; Connection to gifted education origins; Distinction from UDL (responsive vs designed-in)
primary_use_case: K-12 mixed-ability classroom practice; inclusion of gifted, struggling, and English-language-learner students in mainstream classrooms; teacher professional development; foundation for many district-level instructional initiatives; complement to UDL in inclusive-classroom design; widely-cited reference in contemporary teacher education.
common_criticisms: Implementation is genuinely difficult — differentiating content, process, and product simultaneously across 25+ students with varying readiness, interest, and profiles is enormously demanding, and many teachers adopt the language without sustainable practice; empirical evidence on outcome benefits is mixed, with effect sizes often small in studies of typical implementation; 'Learning Profile' has at times included contested learning-styles claims that aren't well empirically supported; can become tracking-by-another-name when 'tiered' assignments cluster low-readiness students together; cognitive-load critics argue that overly varied instruction adds confusion without commensurate learning benefit; tension with curriculum-coverage demands that constrain time for differentiation; commercial certification and consulting ecosystem has shaped adoption.
primary_sources: Tomlinson, C.A. (1995, multiple editions). How to Differentiate Instruction in Mixed-Ability Classrooms; Tomlinson, C.A. (1999, 2nd ed. 2014). The Differentiated Classroom: Responding to the Needs of All Learners

name: Constructivism (Education)
one_line_summary: Learning as active construction of meaning rather than passive reception.
extended_summary: Constructivism in education holds that learners actively construct their own understanding through interaction between new information and prior knowledge, rather than receiving knowledge passively as transmitted content. The educational application descends from cognitive constructivism (Jean Piaget — schemas, assimilation, accommodation; learning through equilibration of cognitive structures) and social constructivism (Lev Vygotsky — zone of proximal development, mediation through cultural tools, learning as social activity preceding individual internalization), with substantial subsequent elaboration by Jerome Bruner (discovery learning, scaffolding, cultural psychology), Seymour Papert (constructionism — learning by building things, particularly via Logo and later programming), and others. The pedagogical implications include emphasis on prior knowledge activation, hands-on and experiential activities, problem-based and inquiry-based methods, social interaction and discourse, scaffolded support, and authentic tasks. Constructivism became dominant in many educational reform movements from the 1980s onward, but has drawn substantial empirical criticism — most prominently in Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark's 2006 'Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work', which argues that constructivist methods underweight the cognitive load demands of novice learners and that direct instruction is empirically more effective than discovery-based methods for most learning contexts. The pedagogy-vs-evidence debate continues actively.
originators: Jean Piaget (cognitive constructivism); Lev Vygotsky (social constructivism); Jerome Bruner (educational application); Seymour Papert (constructionism)
year_or_decade: Mid-20th century (Piaget, Vygotsky); 1960s-90s educational application (Bruner, Papert)
core_components: Knowledge actively constructed by learner; Prior knowledge as foundation; Cognitive constructivism (Piaget — schemas, assimilation, accommodation); Social constructivism (Vygotsky — ZPD, scaffolding, social-then-individual); Constructionism (Papert — learning by making); Discovery and inquiry methods; Authentic tasks and contexts; Distinction from transmission-based instruction; Connection to Inquiry-Based, Project-Based, and Problem-Based Learning
primary_use_case: Foundation for many contemporary pedagogical movements (inquiry-based, project-based, problem-based learning); STEM education reform; technology-enhanced learning (Papert's Logo, contemporary maker education); teacher education and professional development; theoretical underpinning for many instructional-design choices; influence in early-childhood education particularly.
common_criticisms: Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark's 2006 'Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work' (Educational Psychologist) is the canonical empirical critique — argues that constructivist discovery and inquiry methods underweight cognitive load demands of novice learners and that direct instruction outperforms minimal-guidance approaches in most controlled studies; constructivism's commitment to learner-driven discovery can rationalize avoiding necessary direct instruction; substantial gap between epistemological constructivism (which is widely accepted) and pedagogical constructivism (which is empirically contested); cognitive Load Theory (Sweller) provides systematic alternative grounded in working-memory limits; popular constructivist practice often elides the difference between cognitive and social constructivism with substantively different commitments; can become rationalization for under-prepared instruction; the 'discovery vs direct instruction' debate has substantial real-world implications and continuing empirical work.

parent_of: Inquiry-Based Learning; Project-Based Learning; Problem-Based Learning
siblings: Inquiry-Based Learning; Project-Based Learning; Problem-Based Learning; Connectivism

name: Connectivism
one_line_summary: Siemens' learning theory for the digital age emphasizing networks of nodes.
extended_summary: Connectivism was articulated by George Siemens in his 2004 essay 'Connectivism: A Learning Theory for the Digital Age' (and elaborated by Stephen Downes in subsequent work) as a learning theory positioned for digital, networked learning environments. The framework's central claim is that learning is the process of forming and traversing networks of connections — among neurons, among ideas, and among people, technologies, and information sources — and that knowledge resides in the networks rather than in individual minds alone. Siemens articulates principles including: learning may reside in non-human appliances; nurturing and maintaining connections is needed to facilitate continual learning; ability to see connections between fields, ideas, and concepts is a core skill; currency (accurate up-to-date knowledge) is the intent of all connectivist learning activities. Connectivism emerged contemporaneously with the early MOOCs (Siemens and Downes designed the first connectivist MOOC, CCK08, in 2008), and the framework substantially shaped early thinking about online networked learning. Whether connectivism is a genuinely new learning theory or a reinterpretation of social and distributed-cognition frameworks within a digital context remains contested — critics including Verhagen (2006) have argued that connectivism does not meet the criteria for a learning theory but is rather an instructional or curriculum approach.
originators: George Siemens; Stephen Downes (substantial collaborator)
year_or_decade: 2004 (Siemens essay); 2005-2008 (substantial development including first cMOOC)
core_components: Learning as network-formation and traversal; Knowledge in networks (not just minds); Eight principles of connectivism (Siemens 2004); Distinction from constructivism (knowledge construction in mind); Connection to digital and networked learning; Foundation for connectivist MOOCs (cMOOCs); Currency (up-to-date knowledge) as goal; Decision-making as itself a learning process
primary_use_case: Theoretical framework for online and networked learning; foundation for connectivist MOOC design; influence on Personal Learning Networks (PLN) and Personal Learning Environments (PLE); reference framework in digital education research; basis for some emerging online and lifelong-learning practices.
common_criticisms: Verhagen (2006) 'Connectivism: A New Learning Theory?' argued connectivism does not meet criteria for a learning theory (no account of learning mechanism at the individual level) and is better understood as an instructional approach; critics including Bell (2009) argue connectivism is reinterpretation of distributed cognition, social constructivism, and network theory rather than novel; the framework's emphasis on currency over depth has been argued to underweight the value of canonical knowledge that doesn't change rapidly; commercial MOOC platforms (Coursera, edX) have largely been xMOOCs (broadcast model) rather than cMOOCs, suggesting connectivism's pedagogical implications have not driven mainstream adoption; integration with cognitive science is limited; substantial overlap with social constructivism in practice; works principally as digital-age framing rather than as substantively new theory.

name: Andragogy
one_line_summary: Knowles' framework distinguishing adult learning from pedagogy of children.
extended_summary: Andragogy (from Greek aner, 'man,' contrasted with paid, 'child') was substantially codified by Malcolm Knowles in The Modern Practice of Adult Education (1970, revised 1980 as The Modern Practice of Adult Education: From Pedagogy to Andragogy), with the term itself coined earlier by German educator Alexander Kapp in 1833 and revived by Eugen Rosenstock-Huessy in the 1920s. Knowles's framework articulates six assumptions about adult learners that distinguish adult education from child pedagogy: adults need to know why they need to learn something before learning it; adults' self-concept is one of self-direction rather than dependency; adults bring substantial life experience that becomes a resource for learning; adults' readiness to learn is oriented to coping with real-life situations; adults' orientation to learning is task- or problem-centered rather than subject-centered; and adults' motivation is more internal than external. The pedagogical implications include collaborative learning planning, leveraging learner experience, just-in-time relevance, and respect for self-direction. Andragogy has been substantially influential in adult education, corporate training, and professional development. Critics have argued that Knowles's distinctions are not as binary as he presented — children also benefit from relevance and self-direction, while adults sometimes benefit from more structured pedagogy — and that the empirical research grounding the six assumptions is limited.
originators: Malcolm S. Knowles (codification); Alexander Kapp (term coinage 1833); Eugen Rosenstock-Huessy (early 20th century revival)
year_or_decade: 1833 (Kapp coined term); 1970 (Knowles foundational book); 1980 (revised edition)
core_components: Six assumptions about adult learners: need to know, self-concept of self-direction, life experience as resource, readiness oriented to life situations, problem-centered orientation, internal motivation; Distinction from pedagogy (children); Collaborative learning planning; Leveraging learner experience; Self-directed learning; Application to adult education, corporate training, and continuing professional development

name: Experiential Learning
band_notes: Kolb's experiential cycle has more support than the associated learning-styles taxonomy, which has been largely disconfirmed.
one_line_summary: Learning cycle: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, active experimentation.
extended_summary: David Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory was articulated in Experiential Learning: Experience as the Source of Learning and Development (1984), drawing on the work of Kurt Lewin, John Dewey, and Jean Piaget to characterize learning as the process whereby knowledge is created through the transformation of experience. The framework presents a four-stage cycle: Concrete Experience (CE — engaging in a specific activity or experience); Reflective Observation (RO — reviewing and reflecting on the experience); Abstract Conceptualization (AC — drawing conclusions, forming concepts, integrating with prior understanding); Active Experimentation (AE — applying the new understanding in subsequent action). The cycle is iterative — each new experience initiates another round through the four stages. Kolb additionally articulated four learning styles based on individual preferences for combining the dimensions: Diverging (CE+RO), Assimilating (AC+RO), Converging (AC+AE), and Accommodating (CE+AE), assessed through the Learning Style Inventory (LSI). The experiential learning cycle has substantial support and is widely used in adult education, corporate training, and experiential-education programs. The associated learning-styles taxonomy, however, has been largely disconfirmed by mainstream cognitive-psychology research — Pashler et al.'s 2009 'Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence' (Psychological Science in the Public Interest) reviewed the evidence and concluded that matching instruction to claimed learning styles does not improve outcomes. The cycle and the styles must be evaluated separately.

year_or_decade: 1984 (foundational book); 2014 (2nd edition); ongoing development
core_components: Four-stage cycle: Concrete Experience (CE), Reflective Observation (RO), Abstract Conceptualization (AC), Active Experimentation (AE); Iterative cycle through experiences; Two dimensions: grasping experience (CE-AC) and transforming experience (RO-AE); Four learning styles (Diverging, Assimilating, Converging, Accommodating) — empirically contested; Learning Style Inventory (LSI); Connection to Lewin's action research; Distinction between experiential cycle (more supported) and learning styles (largely disconfirmed)

name: Multiple Intelligences
band_notes: Gardner's specific dimensional structure has not been supported by mainstream cognitive psychology research.
one_line_summary: Gardner's framework of distinct intelligences: linguistic, logical, spatial, musical, kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic.
extended_summary: Multiple Intelligences was developed by Howard Gardner at Harvard, presented in Frames of Mind: The Theory of Multiple Intelligences (1983) and elaborated in subsequent works including Intelligence Reframed (1999). Gardner argued that the unitary IQ-based conception of intelligence dominant in psychology was inadequate, and that there are at least seven (later expanded to eight or nine) relatively distinct intelligences: Linguistic, Logical-Mathematical, Spatial, Musical, Bodily-Kinesthetic, Interpersonal, Intrapersonal, Naturalistic (added 1995), and Existential (proposed but not fully accepted by Gardner). Each intelligence was theorized to have distinct neural substrates (supported by selective brain damage), evolutionary origin, developmental trajectory, and exceptional individual exemplars. The framework had enormous influence on education and popular culture, supporting calls for curricular diversity beyond the linguistic-logical bias of conventional schooling. However, Gardner's specific dimensional structure has not been supported by mainstream cognitive psychology research — psychometric studies consistently find that the proposed intelligences correlate substantially (consistent with general intelligence g rather than independent factors), and Gardner's distinction between 'intelligence' and 'talent' has been argued to be definitional rather than empirical. Gardner himself has acknowledged the disconnect, describing MI as 'a set of useful fictions' for educational purposes rather than a validated psychological model. The framework's pedagogical influence persists despite its contested empirical foundations.

year_or_decade: 1983 (Frames of Mind); 1995 (Naturalistic added); 1999 (Intelligence Reframed)

name: Mastery Learning
one_line_summary: Bloom's approach: students must demonstrate mastery before progressing.
extended_summary: Mastery Learning was substantially codified by Benjamin Bloom in his 1968 paper 'Learning for Mastery', extending earlier work by John Carroll on the model of school learning (1963). The framework's central commitment is that virtually all students can achieve mastery of standard curriculum content if given sufficient time and appropriate instruction — and that the principal source of student variation in achievement is variation in time-to-mastery rather than variation in capacity to master. Operationally, mastery learning structures instruction around discrete units, with formative assessment after each unit, corrective instruction (typically through different methods than the original instruction) for students who don't yet demonstrate mastery, and progression to the next unit only after mastery is demonstrated (typically 80-90% on unit assessments). Mastery learning is one of the most empirically-supported instructional approaches — Bloom's 1984 'The 2 Sigma Problem' reported that one-on-one tutoring produced two-standard-deviation improvements over conventional group instruction, with mastery learning capturing roughly half of that effect. Subsequent meta-analyses (Kulik, Kulik & Bangert-Drowns 1990; Guskey 2010) have generally supported substantial positive effects, though smaller than Bloom's original 2-sigma claim. The framework has influenced subsequent personalized learning, competency-based education, and standards-based grading movements.

year_or_decade: 1963 (Carroll's model); 1968 (Bloom's 'Learning for Mastery'); 1984 (Bloom's '2 Sigma Problem' paper)

name: Flipped Classroom
one_line_summary: Direct instruction at home; class time used for application and practice.
extended_summary: The Flipped Classroom inverts the traditional structure of education in which direct instruction (lecture, content delivery) occurs in class and application or practice (homework) occurs at home — instead, students engage with direct instruction (typically through pre-recorded video, readings, or interactive content) before class, freeing class time for application, practice, discussion, and individualized support. The model was substantially developed and popularized by chemistry teachers Jon Bergmann and Aaron Sams at Woodland Park High School in Colorado from 2006-07, who began recording their lectures so absent students could keep up and discovered that the recordings worked well for present students too. Bergmann and Sams's 2012 Flip Your Classroom: Reach Every Student in Every Class Every Day codified the approach. The model gained substantial traction with the rise of online video (Khan Academy launched 2008) and accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic when remote and hybrid learning forced asynchronous content delivery. Empirical evidence on flipped-classroom effectiveness is mixed and substantially dependent on implementation quality — meta-analyses (Cheng et al. 2019; Strelan et al. 2020) show modest positive effects on average, with substantial variation by discipline, age group, and pedagogical practice in the in-class portion. The framework's value depends substantially on what happens during the freed class time — flipped classrooms with passive in-class time are not better than traditional ones.

year_or_decade: 2006-2007 (Bergmann-Sams development); 2012 (Flip Your Classroom book); 2020-21 (COVID-driven acceleration)

name: Project-Based Learning
one_line_summary: Extended student inquiry organized around authentic projects.
extended_summary: Project-Based Learning is the pedagogical approach in which students learn through extended engagement with authentic projects that culminate in publicly-presented products. The framework descends from John Dewey's progressive education tradition and William Heard Kilpatrick's 1918 'The Project Method' (Teachers College Record), with substantial contemporary development through the Buck Institute for Education (now PBLWorks), High Tech High, and other organizations. Modern Project-Based Learning is structured around a Driving Question, sustained inquiry over multiple weeks, authenticity (real-world relevance), student voice and choice, reflection, critique and revision, and a public product. PBLWorks's 'Gold Standard PBL' framework articulates seven essential design elements that distinguish PBL from less rigorous project-based activities. PBL has substantial adoption in K-12 STEM education and in some alternative-school models (notably High Tech High); empirical evidence on outcomes is mixed and substantially dependent on implementation quality, with meta-analyses (Chen & Yang 2019; Condliffe 2017) showing modest positive effects on average with substantial variation. The framework is commonly confused with Problem-Based Learning (different lineage, originally medical-education focused) and with project-based activities that don't meet PBL design standards.

name: Problem-Based Learning
one_line_summary: Learning organized around investigation of complex real-world problems.
extended_summary: Problem-Based Learning was developed at McMaster University Medical School in the late 1960s by Howard Barrows and colleagues, presented in Barrows and Tamblyn's 1980 Problem-Based Learning: An Approach to Medical Education. PBL emerged from concerns that traditional medical education's lecture-and-textbook approach produced graduates with substantial factual knowledge but inadequate clinical reasoning skills. In PBL, students work in small groups (typically 6-10) on complex, ill-structured clinical problems before being taught the relevant content — they identify what they need to learn to address the problem, conduct self-directed research, return to discuss findings, and develop a working diagnosis or solution. The tutor's role is facilitative rather than instructive, asking probing questions and supporting group process rather than delivering content. McMaster's pioneering use spread to medical schools globally, with Maastricht University's adoption in the 1970s being particularly influential, and the framework subsequently extended to other professional education (engineering, business, law) and to some K-12 contexts. PBL is empirically among the most-studied pedagogical innovations in higher education, with extensive evidence including Albanese & Mitchell's 1993 meta-analysis and many subsequent studies — results suggest PBL students show comparable or slightly better long-term retention, improved problem-solving and self-directed learning skills, but somewhat lower performance on traditional content-knowledge assessments compared to conventional curricula.

year_or_decade: Late 1960s (McMaster development); 1980 (Barrows-Tamblyn book); 1970s onward (international spread)

name: Inquiry-Based Learning
one_line_summary: Student-driven exploration with teacher as facilitator rather than transmitter.
extended_summary: Inquiry-Based Learning is the broader category of pedagogical approaches in which students drive their own learning through questioning, investigation, and exploration, with teachers serving as facilitators rather than primary content sources. The framework descends from John Dewey's progressive education (How We Think, 1910) and Jerome Bruner's discovery learning (The Process of Education, 1960), with substantial contemporary development in science education (the 5E Model — Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate, developed by Roger Bybee and the Biological Sciences Curriculum Study). Levels of inquiry are commonly distinguished by who controls the question, procedure, and answer: Confirmation Inquiry (teacher provides all three; student verifies known result); Structured Inquiry (teacher provides question and procedure; student finds answer); Guided Inquiry (teacher provides question; student designs procedure and finds answer); Open Inquiry (student does all three). Inquiry-Based Learning is the umbrella category that includes Project-Based and Problem-Based Learning as more structured variants, but encompasses also less-formal exploration and questioning approaches. Like other constructivist-aligned pedagogies, IBL has been substantially critiqued by cognitive-load research arguing that minimal-guidance approaches underweight novice-learner needs.

year_or_decade: 1910 (Dewey How We Think); 1960 (Bruner Process of Education); 1980s (5E Model); ongoing development

name: TPACK
one_line_summary: Mishra and Koehler's intersecting domains of teacher expertise.
extended_summary: TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) was articulated by Punya Mishra and Matthew Koehler in their 2006 'Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge: A Framework for Teacher Knowledge' (Teachers College Record), extending Lee Shulman's earlier Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) framework (1986). Shulman had argued that effective teaching requires not just Content Knowledge (CK — what teachers know about their subject) and Pedagogical Knowledge (PK — what teachers know about how to teach), but their integration in PCK — knowledge of how to teach this specific content. Mishra and Koehler added the Technology dimension, arguing that effective technology integration similarly requires not just Technology Knowledge (TK), but its integration with content (TCK), pedagogy (TPK), and the full intersection of all three (TPACK). The Venn-diagram representation showing the seven knowledge intersections has become iconic. The framework's central commitment is that effective technology integration is not about technology skills alone but about the integrated knowledge of how specific technologies support specific pedagogical approaches for specific content. TPACK has been substantially influential in teacher education and educational-technology research, particularly in the era of widespread classroom technology adoption.

year_or_decade: 1986 (Shulman PCK foundation); 2006 (Mishra-Koehler TPACK foundational paper)

name: SAMR Model
one_line_summary: Puentedura's four levels of technology integration: substitution, augmentation, modification, redefinition.
extended_summary: The SAMR Model was developed by Ruben Puentedura in the early 2010s as a framework for evaluating how technology is being used in instruction, articulating four progressive levels of integration. Substitution: technology acts as a direct substitute for traditional tools with no functional change (typing instead of handwriting; reading a PDF instead of a printed book). Augmentation: technology substitutes with functional improvement (digital text with embedded definitions; word-processing with spell-check). Modification: technology allows significant task redesign (collaborative document editing; multimedia presentations replacing essay submissions). Redefinition: technology enables previously inconceivable tasks (global student collaboration; immediate worldwide audience for student work). The first two levels represent enhancement; the second two represent transformation. The framework's analytical force is in distinguishing meaningful technology use from technology-as-fancy-substitute, with the implication that transformation-level integration produces greater learning benefit than substitution-level. SAMR has been substantially adopted in K-12 educational-technology professional development and is widely cited alongside TPACK as complementary frameworks. The empirical foundation for the specific four-level hierarchy and its claimed learning benefits is limited — Puentedura's published work is principally consultancy and presentation materials rather than peer-reviewed research, and the framework's iconic status in educational-technology professional development outpaces its empirical validation.

year_or_decade: Early 2010s development; ongoing publication via Puentedura's consultancy

name: Spaced Repetition
one_line_summary: Reviewing material at expanding intervals to optimize long-term retention.
extended_summary: Spaced Repetition is the empirically-validated technique of reviewing learning material at progressively expanding intervals timed to coincide with predicted forgetting, exploiting the spacing effect (better retention from distributed practice than massed practice) first systematically documented by Hermann Ebbinghaus in his 1885 Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology. The technique was operationalized for self-directed learning principally through Sebastian Leitner's flashcard box system (Lerne lernen, 1972 — physical boxes with cards moved between compartments based on recall success) and through Piotr Wozniak's SuperMemo algorithm beginning in 1985, which dynamically computed optimal review intervals based on learner performance. Modern spaced-repetition software (Anki — open-source, descended from SuperMemo; SuperMemo continuing development; Memrise; Quizlet's Long-Term Learning mode; many others) has made the technique broadly accessible, particularly for vocabulary acquisition, medical-school content, and other large memorization workloads. The empirical foundation for the spacing effect is unusually strong by educational-research standards — Cepeda et al.'s 2006 meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin) and the subsequent Cepeda, Vul, Rohrer, Wixted, and Pashler 2008 'Spacing Effects in Learning: A Temporal Ridgeline of Optimal Retention' established the effect across many domains and time scales. Spaced repetition is one of the most empirically-supported study techniques, alongside Active Recall, with which it is typically paired.

name: Active Recall
one_line_summary: Self-testing rather than re-reading to strengthen memory consolidation.
extended_summary: Active Recall (also called Retrieval Practice or the Testing Effect) is the empirically-validated technique of strengthening memory through deliberate retrieval of material from memory, rather than through passive re-exposure (re-reading, highlighting, listening again). The effect was first systematically documented by Edwina Abbott (1909) and substantially developed through the latter half of the 20th century by researchers including Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke. Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 'Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention' (Psychological Science) provided the canonical demonstration: students who studied a passage and then took a test on it remembered substantially more after a week than students who studied the passage twice, despite the test-takers having less total exposure to the material. The mechanism is that retrieval itself is a learning event — the act of pulling information from memory strengthens the retrieval pathway, while passive re-exposure does not. The effect has been replicated across many materials, age groups, and time scales, making it among the most robust findings in educational research. Active Recall is typically paired with Spaced Repetition (Spaced Recall is the most-empirically-supported combination), and is the cognitive mechanism underlying flashcard study, practice-test taking, the Feynman Technique, and many self-quiz tools. Adam Brown's Make It Stick (2014) and Pooja Agarwal's Powerful Teaching (2019) have substantially popularized the research for general audiences and educators.

year_or_decade: 1909 (Abbott); 2006 (Roediger-Karpicke canonical paper); ongoing research
core_components: Active retrieval rather than passive re-exposure; Testing effect (testing enhances long-term retention vs re-study); Free recall, cued recall, and recognition variants; Flashcards, practice tests, self-quizzes as implementation; Integration with Spaced Repetition (Spaced Recall); Mechanism: retrieval as learning event; Distinction from passive study methods (re-reading, highlighting, listening); Connection to Feynman Technique (explanation as retrieval)
primary_use_case: Standard study technique across all learning domains; foundation for many evidence-based teaching practices (frequent low-stakes quizzing, retrieval-based homework); self-directed study (medical school, professional certifications, language learning); pairs with Spaced Repetition for high-volume retention; basis for many learning-app designs; integration with flashcard and practice-test workflows.
common_criticisms: Most effective for retrieval of discrete facts and concepts, less well for understanding-based learning that requires extended reasoning; mechanical retrieval practice can substitute for the deeper engagement that produces understanding; testing-effect claims are sometimes overgeneralized to contexts where the effect is weaker (procedural skills, high-cognitive-load applications); test format matters — recognition tests (multiple choice) produce smaller benefits than free-recall tests; potential test anxiety effects in high-stakes contexts; works best when learners genuinely struggle to retrieve (successful retrieval after substantial effort, not easy recognition); commercial flashcard and quiz industry varies in implementation quality; the term 'active recall' is sometimes used loosely to include any active engagement, diluting the specific evidence base.

name: Feynman Technique
one_line_summary: Test understanding by explaining a concept simply enough for a child.
extended_summary: The Feynman Technique is the practice of testing one's understanding of a concept by explaining it in simple language, as if to someone unfamiliar with the field — typically formulated in four steps: (1) choose a concept and write down what you want to learn about it; (2) explain it in plain language as if teaching it to a child or non-expert; (3) identify gaps where your explanation breaks down or relies on unexplained jargon; (4) review the source material, fill in the gaps, and simplify further. The technique is named for physicist Richard Feynman, whose pedagogical brilliance was widely recognized — he received the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics, taught the iconic Feynman Lectures on Physics (1961-63), and wrote the popular 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!' (1985). However, the named 'Feynman Technique' as a four-step study method does not appear in Feynman's own writings — it is a posthumous attribution that codifies the spirit of his expressed views about understanding and explanation, popularized particularly by James Gleick's biography Genius: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman (1992) and through subsequent self-development popularizations. The cognitive mechanism is well-grounded — the protégé effect (you understand something better when teaching it) and active recall (explanation as retrieval) are both empirically supported — but the specific four-step procedure as 'Feynman's' is folkloric rather than documented.
originators: Richard Feynman (intellectual inspiration); subsequent codifiers in study-skills literature (specific four-step formulation is posthumous)
year_or_decade: Feynman's pedagogical work 1960s-1980s; named 'technique' codification 1990s-2000s in study-skills literature
core_components: Four-step procedure: (1) identify concept; (2) explain in plain language as if to non-expert; (3) identify gaps; (4) review source, simplify further; Connection to protégé effect (teach-to-learn); Connection to active recall (explanation as retrieval); Inspired by but not authored by Feynman; Application across domains; Distinction between the technique-as-practiced and Feynman's own explicit pedagogy

name: Cornell Note-Taking
one_line_summary: Note format dividing the page into cues, notes, and summary sections.
extended_summary: The Cornell Note-Taking System was developed by Walter Pauk at Cornell University in the 1950s, presented in his 1962 How to Study in College (multiple subsequent editions). The format divides each notebook page into three sections: a wide right-hand column (about 6 inches) for taking notes during class or reading; a narrow left-hand column (about 2.5 inches) used afterward for cue-words, questions, and key terms drawn from the notes; and a bottom section (about 2 inches) for a brief summary of the page's content written within 24 hours after the original notes. The system's pedagogical structure encourages active engagement with material at three points: during the lecture or reading (notes column); shortly after, when reviewing notes to identify cues (cue column); and within 24 hours, when summarizing the page (summary section). Subsequent review involves covering the notes column and using the cue column to test recall — operationalizing active recall and spaced review on the same physical page. The system has been substantially adopted in college study-skills programs and in K-12 secondary education, and remains the most-recognized named note-taking format. Empirical research on Cornell-specific outcomes is limited but the underlying practices (active engagement, cue-based review, summarization) are well-supported.
originators: Walter Pauk (Cornell University)
year_or_decade: 1950s development; 1962 (How to Study in College, multiple subsequent editions)

name: Concept Mapping
one_line_summary: Novak's visual representation of relationships among concepts.
extended_summary: Concept Mapping was developed by Joseph Novak and his research group at Cornell University in the early 1970s as a tool to externalize and analyze student conceptual understanding, originally in the context of a longitudinal study of children's learning of science concepts. The method was substantially codified in Novak and Gowin's 1984 Learning How to Learn. A concept map represents knowledge as a labeled directed graph: concepts (typically nouns or noun-phrases) are enclosed in boxes or ovals, and propositions are formed by connecting concepts with labeled lines indicating the relationship (e.g., 'plants → produce → oxygen'). Concept maps are typically organized hierarchically with general concepts at top and specific concepts below, and explicitly distinguish concept nodes from linking phrases. Concept Mapping descends from David Ausubel's assimilation theory of cognitive learning (the principal idea: 'the most important single factor influencing learning is what the learner already knows'), and is intended to make subsumption relationships and meaningful learning explicit. Concept Mapping differs from Mind Mapping (Buzan) in being focused on concept relationships with labeled links, hierarchical organization, and a constructivist learning-theoretic foundation, rather than the radial associative structure of mind maps. Cmap Tools (developed by Novak's IHMC, Florida) is the canonical software implementation. Empirical evidence supports concept mapping's value for conceptual learning, particularly when students construct rather than passively consume maps.

year_or_decade: Early 1970s development; 1984 (Learning How to Learn); 2008 (Novak's Learning, Creating, and Using Knowledge 2nd ed.)
